etymology: American slang recorded from the mid-1950s, meaning to go wild — with rage, with excitement, or with enthusiasm ("the crowd went ape"). The picture is the beast at the zoo rattling its cage. Ape is Old English apa, and the word had long been used for a mimic or a clumsy fool before the teenagers of the 1950s gave it this sense.
biblical_def: When a crowd at a 1957 ball game went ape, they were on their feet and hollering; when a father went ape over a broken window, the neighbours heard it. The phrase pictures a man behaving like the animal in the zoo cage — all noise and no reason. Scripture would say that is exactly the problem, for man is not an ape. Of man the Psalmist says to God, "thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour" (Psa 8:5). A man made in God’s image is meant to govern his passions, not to be governed by them. "A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards" (Pro 29:11). Enthusiasm is no sin — David danced before the LORD with all his might — but rage that turns a man into a beast is. Paul tells young Timothy, "God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind" (2Ti 1:7). And the Spirit grows in God’s people a fruit that no cage can produce: "love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith" (Gal 5:22), "Meekness, temperance" (Gal 5:23). Grandchildren, cheer for your team and laugh out loud at a good joke; joy is a gift. But when you feel the cage rattling inside you, remember whose image you bear, and ask Christ for the sound mind He promised.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (mid-1950s American) for going wild with rage or excitement, like a beast in a cage — but man was made a little lower than the angels (Psa 8:5), and God gives a sound mind (2Ti 1:7).
webster_full: GO APE, phrase (Silent Generation slang, mid-1950s) To go wild with rage, excitement or enthusiasm. "When the home team scored in the ninth, the whole bleachers went ape."

Webster (1828) — APE, noun 1. A genus of quadrupeds, found in the torrid zone of both continents, of a great variety of species. 2. One who imitates servilely, in allusion to the manners of the ape; a silly fellow.
Decode for families: to go wild; we bear God’s image, not the beast’s.
scriptures: Psa 8:5
For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour.
A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards.
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
Gal 5:22
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
Gal 5:23
Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.
corruption_summary: Harmless when it means a cheering crowd; a real sin when it means rage that drops a man below his dignity as the image of God.
corruption_paragraphs: A stadium that goes ape over a home run is simply happy, and there is no reason to frown at it. Scripture is full of shouting and dancing for joy.

The phrase turns dark when it describes fury. It even excuses it, as if a man could not help becoming an animal when provoked. Scripture refuses that excuse. The beasts have no rule over their spirits; men are called to have it, and in Christ they are given it.
roots_summary: Old English apa (ape) → ape (mimic, fool) → mid-1950s go ape (go wild).
roots_lines: Old English apa — ape, monkey
Middle English onward: ape — a mimic; a foolish imitator
Mid-1950s American slang: go ape — go wild with rage or excitement
Scripture: a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards (Pro 29:11)
usage: "The kids went ape when Dad pulled the new Plymouth into the driveway."
A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards (Pro 29:11).
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind (2Ti 1:7).

etymology: From kook, an odd or crazy person, American slang of the late 1950s generally taken as a clipping of cuckoo (crazy, from the bird and its silly call). Kookie (also kooky) became a national word through the hip, comb-wielding parking-lot attendant nicknamed Kookie on television’s 77 Sunset Strip (from 1958), played by Edd Byrnes, and the 1959 novelty record "Kookie, Kookie (Lend Me Your Comb)."
biblical_def: In 1959 kookie meant odd, eccentric, a little crazy — the fellow with the strange hobby, the girl with the wild hat, the neighbour who built a bomb shelter in the back yard. It was usually said with a grin, sometimes with a sneer. Scripture is honest that God’s people often look kookie to the world. When the Lord Jesus began His ministry, even His own friends said, "He is beside himself" (Mar 3:21). When Paul preached the resurrection before a Roman governor, Festus shouted, "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad" (Act 26:24). Paul gladly owned the charge — he called himself a fool for Christ’s sake (1Co 4:10) — because "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1Co 1:27). So a Christian should be slow to call anyone kookie. The odd child in the classroom is "fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:14), and he may be the one God has chosen. Grandchildren, there is a foolishness that is sin — the fool who says in his heart there is no God — and there is a foolishness that is faithfulness. If you follow Christ, someone will think you kookie. Wear it gladly, and never be the one who laughs at the odd kid at the lunch table.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (late 1950s, from kook, likely a clipping of cuckoo) for odd or crazy — a label the world pins on Christ’s people, for God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise (1Co 1:27).
webster_full: KOOKIE, adj. (Silent Generation slang, late 1950s; also kooky; from kook) Crazy, eccentric, odd. "Aunt Ruth’s got some kookie ideas about flying saucers."
Decode for families: odd or crazy; the world called Paul mad, and God chose the foolish things.
scriptures: Mar 3:21
And when his friends heard of it, they went out to lay hold on him: for they said, He is beside himself.
And as he thus spake for himself, Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad.
We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
corruption_summary: Usually a playful word for eccentric, but it can become mockery of the odd and the weak, whom God has a habit of choosing.
corruption_paragraphs: Calling a friend’s idea kookie, with a smile, is no great sin, and a family that laughs at its own odd uncle with affection is a healthy one.

The word turns sharp when it is used to sort people into the normal and the strange, and to shut the strange ones out. That is the spirit of the crowd that called Jesus mad. Teach children that being odd is not the same as being wrong, and that being popular is not the same as being right.
roots_summary: Old French cucu → cuckoo (the bird; a fool) → late-1950s kook (an odd person) → kookie, kooky (crazy, eccentric).
roots_lines: Old French cucu → cuckoo — the bird, named from its call; later, a fool
Early 20th c. American slang: cuckoo — crazy
Late 1950s: kook — an odd or crazy person
1958–59: Kookie on 77 Sunset Strip makes the word national
Scripture: God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise (1Co 1:27)
usage: "Everybody thought Grandpa was kookie for tithing on his first paycheck."
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise (1Co 1:27).
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made (Psa 139:14).

etymology: A rhyming goodbye, answered "after while, crocodile" or "in a while, crocodile," made famous by the song "See You Later, Alligator," written and first recorded by Bobby Charles in 1955 and a hit for Bill Haley & His Comets in 1956. Swing-era jive had already used alligator for a jitterbug, a fan of the music, but the record carried the rhyme into every schoolyard in America. Alligator comes from Spanish el lagarto, the lizard.
biblical_def: A teenager leaving the malt shop in 1956 called out, "See you later, alligator!" and his friends hollered back, "In a while, crocodile!" It was a song first, and then the most cheerful goodbye in America. There is nothing in it but fun — and yet even a goodbye says something about what we expect tomorrow. James gently corrects the easy confidence of every "see you later": "ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour" (Jas 4:14). The Christian habit is to add, "If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that" (Jas 4:15). Solomon said the same: "Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth" (Pro 27:1). That is not gloom; it is trust. The old Christian goodbye was a blessing, and Paul’s farewells are full of it: "Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you" (2Co 13:11). And for those in Christ, every goodbye is only "see you later." Grandchildren, say your rhyme and laugh — and when Grandma and Grandpa leave this world, remember that for believers there is a later, and it is forever with the Lord.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (from the 1955 song, a 1956 hit) for goodbye, answered "in a while, crocodile" — a cheerful farewell Scripture seasons with trust: If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that (Jas 4:15).
webster_full: SEE YOU LATER, ALLIGATOR, interj. (Silent Generation slang, 1955–56; from the song) A rhyming goodbye, answered "After while, crocodile" or "In a while, crocodile." "Gotta run — see you later, alligator!"

Webster (1828) — ALLIGATOR, noun The American crocodile. This animal is of the lizard genus, having a long naked body, four feet, with five toes on the fore feet, and four on the hind, armed with claws, a serrated tail.
Decode for families: a rhyming goodbye; Christians add, If the Lord will.
scriptures: Jas 4:14
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
Jas 4:15
For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.
Pro 27:1
Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.
Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you.
Num 6:24
The LORD bless thee, and keep thee:
corruption_summary: A wholesome, playful goodbye with nothing to correct, only a deeper hope to add.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no sin in a rhyme, and this one has made children giggle for seventy years. Grandparents may teach it to grandchildren with a clear conscience.

The only thing to add is what the rhyme leaves out. Every goodbye assumes a tomorrow we do not own. Christians have long said goodbye with a blessing — God be with you, which is where our word goodbye comes from — and with the hope that, in Christ, no parting is final.
roots_summary: Spanish el lagarto (the lizard) → alligator → swing-era jive (a jitterbug) → 1955–56 rhyme see you later, alligator.
roots_lines: Latin lacertus → Spanish el lagarto — the lizard
16th c. English: alligator — the great reptile of the American rivers
1930s–40s swing jive: alligator — a jitterbug, a fan of the music
1955–56: the song by Bobby Charles, then Bill Haley & His Comets
Scripture: If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that (Jas 4:15)
usage: "Grandpa waved from the station wagon, ‘See you later, alligator!’ and we all yelled back, ‘In a while, crocodile!’"
Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth (Pro 27:1).
The LORD bless thee, and keep thee (Num 6:24).

etymology: Jazz and hipster slang of the 1950s meaning "tell me" or "give it to me" — news, a story, the plain truth, or a handshake ("lay some skin on me"). It grew out of the older lay on in the sense of to deliver or apply, and it passed from the bandstand into teen and campus talk, staying common through the 1960s and 1970s. Lay is Old English lecgan, to set down.
biblical_def: "Lay it on me" was how a hip young man of 1958 said, "Go ahead, tell me — and don’t sugarcoat it." It is the opposite of a man who wants flattery; it asks for the plain truth. Scripture honours that request. "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another" (Eph 4:25). Honest words from a friend may hurt, but they are a kindness: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (Pro 27:6). A man who says "lay it on me" must also be ready to listen to the end: "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him" (Pro 18:13). The best "lay it on me" in the Bible was spoken by a boy in the house of God at night. When the LORD called him, young Samuel answered, "Speak; for thy servant heareth" (1Sa 3:10). Grandchildren, that is the posture of a Christian before the Word of God: open, ready, asking for the truth even when it cuts. God laid the hardest truth on us — that we are sinners — and then laid the best news on us too: that Christ died for sinners. Say "lay it on me" to your Bible every morning, and mean it.
webster_summary: Silent Generation jazz and hipster slang (1950s) for "tell me straight" — a request for plain truth that Scripture honours: speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another (Eph 4:25).
webster_full: LAY IT ON ME, phrase (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; jazz and hipster talk) Tell me; give it to me straight; let me have it. "Bad news from the coach? Lay it on me."
Decode for families: tell me the truth; Samuel said, Speak; for thy servant heareth.
scriptures: Eph 4:25
Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
And the LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel. Then Samuel answered, Speak; for thy servant heareth.
corruption_summary: A wholesome request for honesty; the only danger is asking for the truth without being ready to hear and heed it.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct in lay it on me. It asks for candour, and candour between friends is a Bible virtue. A culture of flattery is far worse than a culture of straight talk.

The phrase can be bravado — a man who says lay it on me and then bristles at the first hard word. Scripture asks for the humility that receives correction. The fool hates reproof; the wise man loves the one who gives it.
roots_summary: Old English lecgan (to lay, set down) → lay on (deliver, apply) → 1950s jazz lay it on me (tell me, give it to me).
roots_lines: Old English lecgan — to lay, to set down
lay on — to apply, to deliver (blows, burdens, words)
1950s jazz and hipster talk: lay it on me — tell me straight; lay some skin on me — shake hands
Scripture: Speak; for thy servant heareth (1Sa 3:10)
usage: "Grandpa put down his paper and said, ‘All right, son, lay it on me.’"
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful (Pro 27:6).
Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour (Eph 4:25).

etymology: Jazz and beat slang of the 1950s: the scene was wherever the action was — the club, the coffeehouse, the party — and to make the scene was to show up there. It grew from scene in the sense of a place where something happens, which goes back through Latin scaena to Greek skene, the tent or stage-building of the theatre.
biblical_def: To a beatnik of 1959, the scene was the place where it was happening — a smoky coffeehouse, a jazz club, a party — and to make the scene was to be there. Nobody wanted to miss it. Scripture agrees that some gatherings must not be missed, but it names a different scene: "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is" (Heb 10:25). The Psalmist made that scene gladly: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD" (Psa 122:1). And the Lord Jesus promised that He Himself would be there: "where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them" (Mat 18:20). No club ever offered a guest list like that. The world’s scenes change every season — "the fashion of this world passeth away" (1Co 7:31) — and the hip places of 1959 are parking lots now. But the gathering of God’s people goes on until He comes. "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God" (Psa 84:10). Grandchildren, there will always be a scene somebody wants you to make. Make the one on the Lord’s Day first; it is the only one where Christ has promised to show up.
webster_summary: Silent Generation jazz and beat slang (1950s) for showing up where things are happening — and Scripture names the gathering not to miss: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together (Heb 10:25).
webster_full: MAKE THE SCENE, phrase (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; jazz and beat talk) To show up; to be where the action is. "Big party at Frank’s Saturday — you going to make the scene?"

Webster (1828) — SCENE, noun [Latin scena; Gr. Heb. The Greek word signifies a tent, hut or cottage. In Latin it is an arbor or stage. The primary sense is to set or throw down.] 1. A stage; the theater or place where dramatic pieces and other shows are exhibited. 2. The whole series of actions and events connected and exhibited; or the whole assemblage of objects displayed at one view.
Decode for families: to show up; the gathering that matters most is the Lord’s house.
scriptures: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
A Song of degrees of David. I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away.
For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
corruption_summary: A harmless phrase for showing up, though the restless chase after wherever the action is can crowd out the gatherings that matter.
corruption_paragraphs: Wanting to be with friends is good, and turning up when you said you would is a virtue. There is nothing wrong with the phrase itself.

What the beat scene taught, though, was a restlessness: the fear of missing something, always moving to the next place. That restlessness is older than the 1950s and alive today. The cure is a settled place to be — a church, a table, a home — where Christ is present and where you are known.
roots_summary: Greek skene (tent, stage) → Latin scaena → scene (place of action) → 1950s make the scene (show up).
roots_lines: Greek skene — a tent; the stage-building of the theatre
Latin scaena → English scene — the place where something happens
1950s jazz and beat talk: the scene — where the action is; make the scene — show up
Scripture: there am I in the midst of them (Mat 18:20)
usage: "Grandma never missed a Sunday; she said that was the one scene worth making."
I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD (Psa 122:1).
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them (Mat 18:20).

etymology: First recorded in Dr. Seuss’s If I Ran the Zoo (1950), where a Nerd is one of the odd creatures the boy imagines collecting; by 1951 Newsweek reported that in Detroit a dull or square person was called a nerd. Whether the slang came from the book is uncertain. The sense of a bookish, socially awkward student came a little later and stuck.
biblical_def: When Grandpa was in high school in 1955, a nerd was a dull, awkward boy — the one with the slide rule and the thick glasses who knew all the answers and none of the dance steps. It was not a kind word. Scripture does not join in the mockery, because it values the very thing the nerd was mocked for. "Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding" (Pro 4:7). Paul told Timothy, "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed" (2Ti 2:15). Daniel and his friends were the bookish boys of Babylon: "God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom" (Dan 1:17). Yet Scripture also guards the studious against their own temptation: "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" (1Co 8:1), and "much study is a weariness of the flesh" (Ecc 12:12) when it is not ruled by the fear of God. The answer for the athlete and the bookworm alike is Christ, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and who loved the clumsy and the clever with the same love. Grandchildren, never sneer at the boy who reads; he may be the next Daniel. And if you are the one who reads, read humbly, and love the ones who do not.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (first in Dr. Seuss, 1950; Detroit teen talk by 1951) for a dull or bookish person — a sneer Scripture refuses, for Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom (Pro 4:7).
webster_full: NERD, n. (Silent Generation slang, early 1950s; first in Dr. Seuss, 1950) A dull, awkward person; later, a bookish, socially clumsy student. "Don’t be a nerd — put the slide rule away and come to the dance."
Decode for families: a bookish kid; Daniel was one, and God gave him wisdom.
scriptures: Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Dan 1:17
As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.
Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
corruption_summary: Born as a sneer at the dull and the studious, the word carries mockery, though later generations wore it with pride.
corruption_paragraphs: Nerd began as an insult, one of the many words a generation used to sort the popular from the awkward. Scripture names that sorting plainly as respect of persons and mockery, and it does not belong in a Christian mouth.

In fairness, the word softened. Many grown men now call themselves nerds with pride, and a family can use it that way. The lasting lesson runs both directions: do not mock the studious, and if you are studious, do not let knowledge puff you up.
roots_summary: 1950 Dr. Seuss’s imaginary Nerd → 1951 Detroit slang (a square, a drip) → 1950s–60s nerd (a dull, bookish person).
roots_lines: 1950: Nerd, an imaginary creature in Dr. Seuss’s If I Ran the Zoo
1951: nerd reported as Detroit slang for a square or a drip
1950s–60s: nerd — a dull, awkward, bookish student
Later decades: worn as a badge by the studious
Scripture: Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1Co 8:1)
usage: "They called Uncle Walt a nerd in ’56; he went on to build radar sets for the Navy."
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom (Pro 4:7).
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed (2Ti 2:15).

etymology: Jazz and beat slang of the 1950s: to call something or someone nowhere ("that cat is strictly nowhere") was to say it was dull, square, out of it — the opposite of gone or hip. The adverb itself is Old English, meaning in no place. The slang echoed into the 1960s, as in the Beatles’ song "Nowhere Man" (1965).
biblical_def: To a hipster of 1958, a party, a song or a person could be nowhere — dull, square, not worth a second look. "That cat is strictly nowhere." It was the cruelest word in the cool vocabulary, because it meant you did not count. Scripture tells us that the Son of God came to earth looking exactly like nowhere. "He hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him" (Isa 53:2). He was raised in a nowhere town: "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?" (Joh 1:46). In His ministry He had no home: "the Son of man hath not where to lay his head" (Mat 8:20). "He is despised and rejected of men" (Isa 53:3). And this is God’s way: "base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are" (1Co 1:28). Grandchildren, the cool crowd will always have a list of people who are nowhere. Look carefully at that list, because Jesus is usually on it, and so are the people He loves. When Nathanael asked whether anything good could come out of nowhere, Philip answered with the best invitation ever given: Come and see.
webster_summary: Silent Generation jazz and beat slang (1950s) for dull, square, out of it — the very verdict the world passed on Christ: Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth? (Joh 1:46).
webster_full: NOWHERE, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; jazz and beat talk) Dull, unhip, out of it; of no account. "That band is strictly nowhere — let’s split."
Webster (1828) — NOWHERE, adverb Not in any place or state. Happiness is nowhere to be found but in the practice of virtue.
Decode for families: a nobody; Jesus came from a nowhere town, and God chooses the despised.
scriptures: Isa 53:2
For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
Joh 1:46
And Nathanael said unto him, Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth? Philip saith unto him, Come and see.
Mat 8:20
And Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
Isa 53:3
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are:
corruption_summary: A word of contempt that wrote people off as worthless, and Scripture overturns it at every turn.
corruption_paragraphs: Applied to a dull song, nowhere is just an opinion. Applied to a person, it is contempt, and contempt for a person made in God’s image is a sin the Bible names plainly. The hip crowd of the 1950s made an art of it.

The gospel turns the word inside out. God made His Son a man of no reputation, and He builds His church out of people the world considered nowhere — fishermen, tax collectors, widows, slaves. A Christian should be the last person to dismiss anyone as nowhere.
roots_summary: Old English no + where (in no place) → nowhere → 1950s jazz and beat nowhere (dull, square, of no account).
roots_lines: Old English — nowhere, in no place
nowhere — figuratively, out of the running, of no account
1950s jazz and beat talk: nowhere — dull, square; the opposite of gone
1965: the echo in the song "Nowhere Man"
Scripture: He is despised and rejected of men (Isa 53:3)
usage: "The kids said the new fellow was nowhere, until Grandpa invited him to supper."
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief (Isa 53:3).
And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen (1Co 1:28).

etymology: American slang recorded from the early 1950s for someone who spoils the fun or leaves a party early; pooper comes from the older slang poop out, to tire out or quit, so the first party pooper was the one too tired to keep going. Party came into English from French partie, a part or side, and Webster in 1828 defined it first as a faction and only sixth as "a select company invited to an entertainment."
biblical_def: In 1953, the party pooper was the fellow who yawned at nine o’clock, wanted the music turned down, or went home before the cake. Nobody wanted to be one. Scripture has a surprising amount to say on both sides. First, God is not a party pooper. The Lord Jesus did His first miracle at a wedding feast in Cana, turning water into wine so the celebration would not end in shame. "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine" (Pro 17:22), and there is "a time to laugh… and a time to dance" (Ecc 3:4). Christians are told to "Rejoice with them that do rejoice" (Rom 12:15), which means a sour face at a friend’s happy day is a small failure of love. But there is another side. Some parties ought to be left early. "My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not" (Pro 1:10). The believer who walks out of the wrong kind of party will be called worse names than party pooper: "they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you" (1Pe 4:4). Grandchildren, be the first to laugh at a good feast and the first to leave a wicked one. The Lord who made the wine at Cana will one day sit with His people at the marriage supper of the Lamb — the best feast there will ever be.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (early 1950s American) for a killjoy who spoils the fun — though Scripture says there is a time to laugh and a time to refuse: My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not (Pro 1:10).
webster_full: PARTY POOPER, n. (Silent Generation slang, early 1950s; from poop out, to tire and quit) A killjoy; one who spoils the fun or leaves a party early. "Don’t be a party pooper — stay for one more song."

Webster (1828) — PARTY, noun [Latin pars. See Part .] 1. A number of persons united in opinion or design, in opposition to others in the community. 6. A select company invited to an entertainment; as a dining party a tea party an evening party
Decode for families: a killjoy; laugh at the good feast, and leave the wicked one.
scriptures: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
Ecc 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
Pro 1:10
My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not.
Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you:
corruption_summary: A playful word that is usually harmless, but the fear of being called one has pushed many young people to stay at parties they should have left.
corruption_paragraphs: A genuine killjoy — the one who sulks at every celebration — does deserve a gentle nudge. Joy at a wedding, a birthday or a homecoming is right, and Scripture commands it.

The word does its real damage as a weapon. It shames the one who says no, and it has kept many a teenager at a party long after the drinking started. Teach children that the name is cheap and their conscience is not; Christ will honour the one who walked out.
roots_summary: French partie (a part, a side) → party (a company; later, a social gathering) + poop out (to tire, quit) → early-1950s party pooper.

party — a faction; a side; a select company invited to an entertainment
Earlier 20th c. American slang: poop out, pooped — to tire, to quit; worn out
Early 1950s: party pooper — a killjoy
Scripture: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine (Pro 17:22)
usage: "Grandma was no party pooper — she danced the Lindy at every wedding till she was eighty."

etymology: Peepers for "eyes" is long-standing English slang, centuries older than the Silent Generation, from peep, to look slyly or through a small opening. That generation knew it best from the 1938 song "Jeepers Creepers" (music by Harry Warren, words by Johnny Mercer), which asks a girl where she got "those peepers," and it stayed a fond, joking word for eyes through the 1940s and 1950s.
biblical_def: When a crooner of 1938 asked a girl where she got "those peepers," the whole country hummed along, and Grandpa was still calling Grandma’s eyes her peepers fifty years later. It is a fond, homely word. Scripture has a great deal to say about the eyes, because they are the windows through which the heart is filled. "The light of the body is the eye" (Mat 6:22). Job made a solemn promise about his: "I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?" (Job 31:1). That is a word for every young man. The best use of our peepers is to look to God: "Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law" (Psa 119:18). And we should remember that our eyes are not the only ones watching: "The eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the evil and the good" (Pro 15:3). That is a warning to the wicked and a comfort to the faithful. Grandchildren, God gave you your peepers as a gift. Use them to read His Word, to see the beauty of His world, and to notice the people around you who need help. And if you trust in Christ, one day you will use them to see Him face to face.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (older English slang, made famous by a 1938 song) for the eyes — a fond word for a gift Scripture bids us guard: I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid? (Job 31:1).
webster_full: PEEPERS, n. pl. (old English slang; a Silent Generation favourite after a 1938 song) The eyes. "Close those peepers, young man — it’s past bedtime."
Decode for families: eyes; Job made a covenant with his, and David prayed for God to open his.
scriptures: Mat 6:22
The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
Job 31:1
I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?
Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.
Pro 15:3
The eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.
corruption_summary: A wholesome, affectionate word for eyes; the only lesson is the one Scripture attaches to the eyes themselves — guard them.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in peepers. It is a grandparent’s word, said at bedtime and over a baby’s crib, and it is full of affection.

The word does open a door to one of Scripture’s plainest teachings: the eyes lead the heart. The song that made it famous was a young man admiring a girl’s eyes, which is innocent enough; but a covenant with the eyes, like Job’s, is what keeps admiration from becoming lust.
roots_summary: peep (to look slyly, through a small opening) → peeper (one who peeps) → slang peepers (the eyes) → 1938 song and 1940s–50s fond use.

peeper — one who peeps; slang plural peepers, the eyes

1940s–50s: peepers — a fond family word for eyes
Scripture: The light of the body is the eye (Mat 6:22)
usage: "Grandpa still says Grandma has the prettiest peepers in Ohio."
Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law (Psa 119:18).

etymology: Shook up (nonstandard for shaken up) meant upset or agitated; Elvis Presley’s 1957 number-one hit "All Shook Up," written by Otis Blackwell, made it the phrase of the year, though there it meant the trembling of a young man in love. The participle shook for shaken is old and regional; shake is Old English sceacan.
biblical_def: In 1957 every teenager in America was singing that he was all shook up, and the phrase stuck for anything that rattled you: bad news, a near miss on the highway, a scare at the doctor’s office. "She was pretty shook up after the accident." Scripture knows the feeling well, and it knows the cure. The Psalmist pictured the whole world shaking and still sang, "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble" (Psa 46:1). David, hunted by enemies, said, "He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved" (Psa 62:2). When the disciples were shook up in a storm on the lake, the Lord Jesus "rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm" (Mar 4:39). And to frightened men on the night before His death He said, "Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid" (Joh 14:27). Grandchildren, you will be shook up many times in this life, and that is no sin. The question is where you run when the ground moves. Everything in this world can be shaken, but believers are "receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved" (Heb 12:28). Run to the King of that kingdom.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (made famous by a 1957 hit song) for upset or rattled — a common trouble with an old cure: He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved (Psa 62:2).
webster_full: SHOOK UP, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; from nonstandard shook for shaken; "All Shook Up," 1957) Upset, agitated, rattled; in the song, trembling with love. "Mom was all shook up after the fender-bender."
Decode for families: rattled; the Lord says, Peace, be still.
scriptures: Psa 46:1
To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, A Song upon Alamoth. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
Psa 62:2
He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved.
Mar 4:39
And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear:
corruption_summary: A plain, honest phrase for being upset, with nothing sinful in it; the only question is where the shaken heart runs.
corruption_paragraphs: Being shook up is not a sin. The Lord Jesus Himself was troubled in spirit, and the Psalms are full of men whose hearts were shaken. The slang names a real human experience honestly.

If there is anything to watch, it is the song’s use, which made romantic feeling into a kind of helpless fever. Feeling is not the master of a Christian; Christ is. Whether the shaking comes from fear or from infatuation, the believer brings it to the One who calms storms.

shook — old and regional past participle for shaken
1957: "All Shook Up," written by Otis Blackwell, a number-one hit for Elvis Presley
1950s: shook up — upset, rattled
Scripture: Peace, be still (Mar 4:39)
usage: "After the twister missed the farm by a mile, Grandpa was shook up for days — then he held a thanksgiving supper."
God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble (Psa 46:1).
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you (Joh 14:27).

etymology: From the air war of the Second World War, when a pilot or plane brought down by enemy fire was shot down; the phrase then passed into civilian slang for being rejected or refused — an idea shot down in a meeting, a boy shot down when he asked a girl to the dance. The date of the figurative sense is uncertain; it was in use by the mid-20th century. Shoot is Old English sceotan.
biblical_def: The men who came home from the war knew what shot down meant: the plane that did not return, the crew listed as missing. When their younger brothers used the phrase in 1956, it meant something smaller — a boy asked a girl to the sock hop and got shot down. Every one of us has been shot down, and it stings. Scripture does not pretend rejection is nothing. But it shows us that the Son of God was rejected before any of us: "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief" (Isa 53:3). "The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner" (Psa 118:22). What the world turned down, God raised up. That is why a Christian can survive rejection. Even if those closest to us turn away, "When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up" (Psa 27:10). Paul, who was driven out of city after city, wrote, "Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed" (2Co 4:9). And the best promise of all comes from Christ Himself: "him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out" (Joh 6:37). Grandchildren, people will shoot you down. Christ never will. And when you have to say no to someone, say it kindly; you know how it feels.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (from Second World War air combat) for being rejected or turned down — a sting Christ knew first, and His promise answers it: him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out (Joh 6:37).
webster_full: SHOT DOWN, adj. (Silent Generation slang, from Second World War air combat) Rejected, refused, turned down. "Asked Peggy to the hop and got shot down flat."
Decode for families: turned down; Christ was rejected so that He would never reject those who come to Him.
scriptures: Isa 53:3
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.
Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed;
Joh 6:37
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
corruption_summary: A neutral, even honest phrase for the pain of rejection; its only weakness is that it makes every refusal sound like a death.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with the phrase, and it carries an honourable memory: the airmen of the Second World War, many of whom never came home. A family that uses it can pause to remember them.

The figurative use can magnify small rejections into catastrophes, as if a girl’s no or a boss’s refusal were the end of a man. Scripture puts them in proportion. Our worth is settled by God’s acceptance in Christ, not by any human yes or no.
roots_summary: Old English sceotan (to shoot) → shot down (brought down by fire, Second World War aviation) → mid-century slang (rejected, refused).

Scripture: The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner (Psa 118:22)
usage: "Grandpa got shot down three times before Grandma said yes — she says she was testing him."
Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed (2Co 4:9).
When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up (Psa 27:10).

etymology: Jazz and teenage slang of the 1950s for music, especially recorded music ("spin some sounds," "crazy sounds"), from the plain noun sound. Disc jockeys and record shops used it, and it carried into the 1960s. Sound in this sense comes through Old French son from Latin sonus; it is a different word from sound meaning whole and healthy, which is Old English.
biblical_def: When a teenager of 1957 said, "Let’s go over to Jimmy’s and hear some sounds," he meant records — the new 45s on the hi-fi, or a jazz combo at the club. The word was cool and a little detached, as if music were just noise you liked. Scripture treats music as one of God’s great gifts and calls for it to be offered back to Him. "Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp" (Psa 150:3). The Psalms command skill and joy together: "Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise" (Psa 33:3). Music has real power over the soul; when David played the harp for troubled Saul, "Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him" (1Sa 16:23). Because it is powerful, it matters what sounds we feed on. Paul tells the church to be "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord" (Eph 5:19). And all of it has one end: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD" (Psa 150:6). Grandchildren, our generation went from the big bands to rock and roll, and some of those sounds lifted us and some dragged us down. Love good music, play it well, and let the best sounds in your house be the songs you sing to Christ.
webster_summary: Silent Generation jazz and teen slang (1950s) for music, especially records — a gift Scripture calls us to offer back to God: Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp (Psa 150:3).
webster_full: SOUNDS, n. pl. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; jazz and teen talk) Music, especially records. "Bring your 45s over and we’ll spin some sounds."

Webster (1828) — SOUND, noun 1. Noise; report; the object of hearing; that which strikes the ear; or more philosophically, an impression of the effect of an impression made on the organs of hearing by an impulse or vibration of the air, caused by a collision of bodies or by other means; as the sound of a trumpet or drum; the sound of a human voice; a horrid sound; a charming sound; a sharp sound; a high sound
Decode for families: music; the best sounds are the songs we sing to the Lord.
scriptures: Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp.
Psa 33:3
Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise.
And it came to pass, when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD.
corruption_summary: A neutral word for music; the only concern is the one Scripture raises about music itself — it shapes the heart, for good or ill.
corruption_paragraphs: Sounds is a harmless word, and the love of music behind it is a good gift. The church has always sung, and the grandparents who swayed to the big bands were enjoying something God made.

Calling music mere sounds does flatten it a little, as if it were noise to be consumed. Music carries words and moods into the soul, and a family should choose it as carefully as it chooses friends. Some sounds stir worship; some stir lust or rage. Scripture asks us to know the difference.
roots_summary: Latin sonus (sound) → Old French son → English sound (noise, tone) → 1950s plural sounds (music, records).
